HUM 1024.title: Introductory Humanities: Great Books
HUM 1024.description: An introduction to the humanities through the topic of “Great Books.” Students will closely analyze primary canonical texts from the West and from the global south. Political, religious, philosophical, and literary works by important writers and communities from across the globe will be explored to understand the human condition and self-formation. Such engagement with primary texts will be put into the context of larger topics such as class, race, and gender in addition to colonialism, decolonialism, and postcolonial modernity.

HUM 1054.title: Virginia Tech Prison Book Project
HUM 1054.description: A one-hour course with the Virginia Tech Prison Book Project. Students will complete a learning module about carceral institutions in the United States and the impact of educational opportunities on the lives of incarcerated people. They will then participate in a service learning event where they match individual requests from incarcerated readers to books and prepare the books for shipping.

HUM 1064.title: The Culture of Money
HUM 1064.description: Exploration of the cultural, religious, and ethical dimensions of money and related topics, such as gifting, markets, the charging of interest, charity, pricing strategies, private property, and wage labor. Comparison of the disparate forms and uses of money and how money has worked in various cultural and historical frameworks. Evaluation of the differences between capitalist and non-capitalist money-systems, including philosophical debates about the relationship between money and human nature. Examination of ethical issues pertaining to money, such as the forgiveness of debt, money’s impact on social inequality, and the role of money in various projects of political empowerment and disempowerment.

HUM 1074.title: Ghosts
HUM 1074.description: Fundamental humanities and social scientific frameworks underlying belief in ghosts and the paranormal as sites of human meaning-making and as expressions of cultural norms and anxieties concerning human behavior and social relationships, especially in US contexts pertaining to enslavement, displacement, and gender disparity. Introduces students to key concepts and methods such as auto-ethnography, the study of material culture, historical criticism, and literary criticism via an appealing and engaging topic. Training in ethical self-assessment and assessment of human meaning-making and behavior concerning ghosts and the paranormal such as affect theory, empiricism, and experience.

HUM 1504.title: Introduction to Popular Culture
HUM 1504.description: The development and formation of the category of popular culture. Competing theories and methods for analyzing popular culture. Activities, objects, and ideas included under the rubric of popular culture. Critical thinking about the production of popular culture in relation to race, gender, class, and other forms of human difference.

HUM 1604.title: Introduction to Humanities and the Arts
HUM 1604.description: Explores the written, visual, and performing arts of selected periods and cultures, setting them in the context of their times. Study of these periods linked with overarching questions of cultural encounters, interactions, and negotiations. Introduces principles of each art form as well as the means of appreciation. Students taught methods in researching, writing, and presenting on these art forms.

HUM 1704.title: Introduction to Appalachian Studies
HUM 1704.description: Introduces students to the history of the Appalachian region from European contact to the present. Traces the idea of Appalachia by tracing ways in which Americans have imagined the region over time. Explores humanistic problems of cultural identity, race and ethnicity, place and globalization, and impacts of natural resource extraction.

HUM 2104.title: Oral Traditions and Culture
HUM 2104.description: Examination of the worlds great oral traditions, both ancient and contemporary. Emphasis on performance contexts, relationships among multicultural traditions, including American Indian oral traditions, and the relationships among orality, literacy, technology, media, and culture.

HUM 2204.title: The Creative Process
HUM 2204.description: Explores ways in which creativity and design can be understood historically as well as understood and practiced in a classroom setting. Subjects include any or all of the following: theories of creativity; traditions associated with understanding and making several kinds of art; studying artworks from different cultural backgrounds, working with the limitations and possibilities inherent in design projects, and examining how and why they were created; and preparing final creative projects for classroom presentation.

HUM 2244.title: Campus Free Speech
HUM 2244.description: Historical, religious, philosophical, and legal frameworks that shape modern debates on campus free speech and academic freedom. Focusing on case studies this course offers a non-partisan examination of hate speech codes, speaker shout-downs, ideological diversity, university neutrality, the limits of academic freedom, and other issues relevant to students, faculty, and administrators at public and private US universities. Students will engage in practical training in civil and respectful deliberation about matters of law and policy, the pursuit of truth, and the pursuit of permissive versus censorious approaches to campus speech.

HUM 2404.title: Folk Cultures in Appalachia
HUM 2404.description: Examination of the expressive genres and cultural processes of communities in Appalachia. Documentation of art and skill in everyday life, including material culture (e.g., foodways, architecture), customary behavior (e.g., music, ritual, occupational practice), and verbal art (e.g., narrative, speechplay), and analysis of how people have used these forms to shape social identities, physical spaces, and power relations.

HUM 2504.title: Introduction to American Studies
HUM 2504.description: Methodology and tools of American studies, with a focus on developing analytic skills to assess discourse across varied media. Interdisciplinary investigation of histories, politics, cultures, and beliefs in the Americas, including the impacts of encounter and exchange. Intensive study of a specific topic or period.

HUM 3034.title: Theories of Popular Culture
HUM 3034.description: Examination of theories for understanding the ways in which popular objects and practices (such as television programs, films, or attending sporting events) represent, maintain, and contest societal norms, including norms regarding gender and sexuality, race and ethnicity, and class and place, with an emphasis on the United States.

HUM 3034H.title: Theories of Popular Culture
HUM 3034H.description: Examination of theories for understanding the ways in which popular objects and practices (such as television programs, films, or attending sporting events) represent, maintain, and contest societal norms, including norms regarding gender and sexuality, race and ethnicity, and class and place, with an emphasis on the United States.

HUM 3204.title: Multicultural Communication
HUM 3204.description: Exploration of communication in and among various cultural groups through an examination of communicative practices, registers, discourse, and performance. Emphasis on understanding cultural differences and similarities in the different styles and stances in communication and their meanings to participants.

HUM 3204H.title: Multicultural Communication
HUM 3204H.description: Exploration of communication in and among various cultural groups through an examination of communicative practices, registers, discourse, and performance. Emphasis on understanding cultural differences and similarities in the different styles and stances in communication and their meanings to participants.

HUM 3464.title: Appalachian Communities
HUM 3464.description: The concept of community in Appalachia using an interdisciplinary approach and experiential learning. Interrelationships among geographically, culturally, and socially constituted communities, public policy, and human development. Pre: Junior standing.

HUM 4124.title: Topics in Culture
HUM 4124.description: Uses sociological, anthropological, as well as artistic and humanist paradigms to analyze culture. Discusses 20th and 21st century cultural trends. Analyzes the implications of social context for cultural artifacts such as art. Topics are variable. Example topics include the cultural construction of race and the cultural of the nineteen sixties. Course may be repeated with different course content for up to 6 credits. Pre: Junior or Senior standing.
HUM 4124.prereq: SOC 1004 or SOC 1014 or AFST 1714 or AINS 1104 or RLCL 1004 or RLCL 2004 or WGS 1824

HUM 4414.title: Issues in Appalachian Studies
HUM 4414.description: Research conducted by students on issues relevant to local or regional sustainability in contemporary Appalachia on contemporary environmental and community issues. Focus on environmental justice ethical issues expressed in or created by various forms of discourse.

HUM 5104.title: Historical and Theoretical Frameworks in Material Culture and Public Humaniti
HUM 5104.description: Study of the theoretical frameworks and historiographic debates that inform the contemporary research and writing of material culture and public humanities. Investigation of methodologies ranging from Marxism to postmodernism with specific application to cultural objects situated in the public sphere. Prerequisite: Graduate Standing required.

HUM 5204.title: Research Methods in Material Culture and Public Humanities
HUM 5204.description: Introduction to skills and methods used in the research, writing and publication on material culture and public humanities. Pre: Graduate Standing.

HUM 5304.title: Material Culture and Humanities in the Public Sphere
HUM 5304.description: Advanced seminar on material culture and humanities in the public sphere through an examination of humanistic approaches to civic spaces, applying critical turns to public debates. Graduate Standing required.

HUM 5584.title: Topics in Public Humanities
HUM 5584.description: Advanced seminar on topics in public humanities, ranging from an exploration of how various humanities disciplines relate to public issues and concerns, to a study of region, regionalism, and place in public humanities. May be repeated with different topic content for a maximum of 9 credits. Prerequisite: Graduate Standing required.
